newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission urges fight against Internet abuse.
newsitem.headline: Commission urges fight against Internet abuse.

text.p: European Union governments, industry groups and parents should unite to fight child pornography and other illegal or harmful material on the Internet, the European Commission said on Wednesday.

The Commission, under pressure to act in the wake of a child-sex scandal in Belgium, issued two reports on ways to protect children and to prevent criminals, such as terrorists, from misusing the global computer network.

It shied away from proposing strict legislation, however, instead offering solutions such as industry codes of conduct, cooperation between the 15 EU governments to enforce existing laws and software that can screen out unwanted material.

Governments should consider, however, whether an EU legal framework was needed to clarify whether companies that offer Internet access or services are liable for illegal content -- for example, child pornography, copyright infringements, libel or fraudulent offers, it said.
That question has been an issue in Germany, which required the U.S. online service provider CompuServe to block access to certain Internet "newsgroups" that it said were illegal.
The Commission said that approach did not solve the problem, however, since criminals can "hop" from one Internet communications mode to another if they are blocked.
The question of child pornography has been thrown in the spotlight in recent months following the deaths of four girls in Belgium that were linked to a paedophile network.

The EU's Telecommunications Council agreed to a request by Belgian Telecommunications Minister Elio di Rupo last month to intensify its effort to find ways to keep material featuring sexual abuse or exploitation of children off the Internet.
The Commission stressed that it was trying to find solutions that did not threaten freedom of expression.
"We are not proposing a measure that could be misconstrued as censorship," Industrial Affairs Commissioner Martin Bangemann told a news conference.
He said there was no need to lay down a "huge raft of legislation" to define which Internet content is illegal since existing laws about criminal activity would already apply.
But he said EU states should agree on some kind of minimum definition tailored to the Internet.
The Commission said action was needed to cut down on anonymous use of the Internet and that industry codes of conduct should guarantee that all material on the network is traceable.
"We have to be able to identify suppliers in all cases," Bangemann said. "Otherwise it's impossible to prosecute."
The reports also highlighted a new technical standard known as PICS, the Platform for Internet Content Selection, that allows data on the network to be labelled and filtered out.
The Commission said Europe should develop its own rating systems, rather than rely on those used by the United States.

The Industry Council agreed last week that Germany should host an international conference of law enforcement authorities and industry officials to discuss whether to draw up a global convention on illegal and harmful content on the Internet.

The Commission adopted two reports -- a Green Paper on the protection of minors and human dignity in audiovisual and information services drawn up by Culture Commissioner Marcelino Oreja and a Communication on illegal and harmful content on the Internet drawn up by Bangemann.
The green paper launches a consultation process on ways to protect minors from material on the Internet and new television services such as pay-per-view.
It asks interested parties to comment on nine key questions covering three themes: legal protection, parental control systems and international cooperation.
The communication proposes short-term measures that can be taken to fight the use of the Internet to disseminate illegal materials, including child pornography.
The Telecommunications Council will rely on the communication when it discusses the question in November.

It has also asked a working party -- which includes of representatives of the 15 EU telecoms ministries and companies that provide access to online services or prepare the content -- to make concrete proposals before then.
The green paper is the first installment of a document that Oreja promised during the debate over revising the EU's Television Without Frontiers directive.
Rather than apply rules in that directive -- such as quotas on foreign programming or measures to protect children -- to new media services, Oreja agreed to draft a green paper on the question.
He told the news conference the second installment would cover the question of "cultural diversity" -- that is, how to prevent U.S. domination of programmes.
